paragraphs: At seventeen, Helai A-Luo got into a fight at the commandery school in Ye.

The ink in the classroom was still wet that morning. The instructor had just finished a lesson on the Household Statutes and called on each student to state his registered household. A-Luo stood toward the back in a blue-green robe sewn by his mother. When the name “Helai” was read out, a student surnamed Fu turned around, hid his mouth behind his sleeve and laughed.
“Dressed like a Han man, yet born with a Xianbei name.”
A-Luo lowered his eyes and ignored him.
The boy went on. “I hear that when his father died, they nearly took all eighty mu of his family’s land. It took the Heavenly King himself to acknowledge who his father was.”

A-Luo sprang from his mat and struck the boy hard enough to bloody his nose. His opponent lunged at him, and together they knocked over a shelf, scattering bamboo slips across half the room. The instructor arrived and had the slips collected before ordering them both into the lecture hall. A-Luo’s lip was badly swollen. The Fu boy, tears streaming down his face, still pointed at him and cried, “A barbarian never changes his ways.”

The instructor, surnamed Pei, had hair already half gray. Once a copyist in the service of Former Yan, he had taught at the commandery school for more than ten years after that kingdom fell. He knew well that a quarrel between boys often concealed grudges among their fathers and brothers. He did not immediately reach for his ruler. Instead he asked the Fu boy, “What did you say to him?”
The boy did not answer.

“Then you may begin with this morning’s lesson. Copy the Household Statutes twice and bring them to me tomorrow. A-Luo has injured a fellow student, so he shall also copy the section on assault and injury. After that, the two of you will set the bookshelves right.”
“Master, he spoke about my father—” A-Luo began.
“Are your father’s military-service fields still in your household?”
“Yes.”
“Has the county issued your mother’s wheat seed for this year?”
“It has.”
“Can two boys quarreling erase your father’s name from the military register?”

A-Luo was silent. At ten, he had walked a very long way with his mother, carrying his father’s little horse saddle against his chest. The clan had a sword, the Zhao family a broken-down house, and every household seemed to say that half of him belonged somewhere else. In the end the Department of State Affairs had consulted the old military records and acknowledged his inheritance. The document was kept in the county archive, and the fields were theirs. A-Luo knew all this. He also knew why a single remark could still make him strike.

Seeing him lower his head, the instructor told both boys to put every scattered slip back in its case. “If you still wish to fight today, finish fighting before you come to learn your characters. My wages for teaching have nothing to do with which ancestors earned merit in which battles.”

That afternoon an express rider arrived at the school from Weichang County. Several hundred people had gathered with hoes along the north canal southeast of the county seat, facing one another across the banks. An elderly man had already been shoved from a field ridge. The county lacked clerks who could speak Xianbei and requested students from the commandery school to help with questioning. Instructor Pei thought for a moment and chose A-Luo.
“Your family’s fields lie there too.”
“All the more reason I may take sides if I go.”
“You are going to interpret, not judge the case. If you cannot stop yourself speaking for your own family first, come back and receive a beating from my ruler.”

With the official paper in hand, A-Luo rode east aboard a relay cart belonging to merchants from Guzang. Their wagons carried felt, iron hoops and a bundle of dried herbs. Inspection vouchers from several checkpoints hung at their waists. The leader, a short-mustached man surnamed Kang, spoke Chinese with the accents of Liangzhou mixed into it. A-Luo asked how much less the journey from Guzang to Ye cost than before.

“There are fewer government charges at each pass. Men who want private money haven’t lost any of their appetite for it, though.” Kang stuffed a sheaf of crumpled papers back into his robe. “Only now, with one contract, you can find the office and demand an answer. Even a grasping clerk has to think twice before putting out his hand. To me, that is worth half a bolt of silk.”

A-Luo laughed as he listened. At the Weichang relay post the station keeper counted the iron goods honestly and asked no extra payment. As Kang left, he looked back twice, hardly believing a checkpoint could be passed so easily.
The people of Xinmin Ward, the New Citizens' Ward, were in no mood for such good humor.

After the great flood in Hebei, several low-lying villages had been destroyed. The county had redistributed fields on higher ground, placing former Yan military households beside discharged soldiers from Guanzhong and landless Qiang families. They called the settlement Xinmin, “New Citizens,” but the old people did not care for the name. “The people of Yan have lived here for generations. What is new about us?” “The Guanzhong military registers are worn out already. What is new about them?” Only the children, accustomed to new houses and canals, never asked which county clerk had invented the ward’s name.

When A-Luo reached the north canal, both sides of the old sluice were crowded with people. Water seeped in threads through the joints of the wooden boards, and the mud at the canal bed had turned pale. Upstream, Lü Yan stood beside the winch gripping a spade, surrounded by Guanzhong military households whose men had followed the Fu family through years of campaigning. Downstream, Tuoba Lin had gathered former Yan families; long poles and hoes lay at their feet. By the farthest branch ditch, Liang Wuzhi of the Qiang leaned on a crutch and cursed in rough anger. His wheat had seen no water for three days, and its leaves curled like scraps of paper.
“The eastern ditch was due to open at dawn!” Tuoba Lin shouted.
“Because you say it’s due, I must open it?” Lü Yan struck the sluice post. “I let water through upstream for only two hours. The wind was fierce last night. Not an inch stayed in the paddies.”
“Your family grows rice, so my wheat must die of thirst?”
“The court supplied that rice seed too!”

One man invoked the ancestral achievements of those who had dug the canal under Yan. Another shouted back that Guanzhong soldiers had conquered Hebei for the court. Liang Wuzhi brought his crutch down hard on the stone steps. “Let a little reach the southern mouth first! By the time you finish arguing, there’ll be no life left in the shoots!”
A young military-household man turned to him and cursed. “Yao Chang is dead, and you people still have the face to fight us for water!”

Liang Wuzhi’s face went ashen. He had not joined Yao’s army at White Horse Slope; his son-in-law had even carried wounded Qin soldiers. Yet someone still used Yao Chang’s name to beat him down. He moved forward two steps on his crutch. “Do my wheat plants know Yao Chang? And when your roof collapsed that year, who helped lift your beams?”

A-Luo climbed quickly onto a rock, asking Tuoba Lin in Xianbei to put down his hoe, then calling out in Chinese that the magistrate was on his way. Lü Yan looked at him. “Your mother’s fields are downstream. Don’t start demanding water for her.”
“I am only here to interpret,” A-Luo answered.
“Then tell them to speak like human beings!”
“They understand you perfectly well.”

At that, several men could not help giving half a laugh. The crowd had yet to disperse when Suo Gong, magistrate of Weichang, arrived with two field assessors and a dozen runners. Suo Gong had once served as a clerk in Liangzhou. After its fall, he had been transferred several times before finally securing a county magistracy at Weichang. Locals said he knew nothing of Hebei’s canals, while the Guanzhong military households disliked his western accent. He rode up and, without asking anyone’s tribe, ordered them all to surrender their bows.
“Keep the hoes. We need those to repair the sluice. But the bows go. Whoever looses the first arrow will be the first I arrest.”

Lü Yan laid his bow on the ground, and Tuoba Lin ordered his followers to do the same. Suo Gong crouched beside the old sluice and scraped away the outer planking with the tip of his knife. Beneath the freshly nailed veneer, the core was rotten through; a finger’s touch broke it into crumbs.
“Who signed for the replacement timber reported delivered last year?”
The waterworks officer Feng, clutching the canal accounts, hurried forward. “I inspected it, Your Honor. Not all the wood arrived, and some was washed away by the current.”
“The accounts say it all arrived.”
“The entry was mistaken.”

Suo Gong turned to the back of the ledger. Several thin sheets fell out. They recorded grain and money collected under separate headings: Guanzhong military households, former Yan households and Qiang households, with different levies for each. Tuoba Lin recognized the two dou of millet he had paid. Lü Yan discovered that the upstream farmers had also been charged “sluice-protection money.” Liang Wuzhi produced a small wooden token, the receipt for a “supplementary registration levy” secretly collected by Officer Feng.
“The household register already lists everyone on the same page,” Suo Gong said. “Yet you have put them back into three or four different books so you can demand money from each.”

Feng hastened to protest that the wards had voluntarily contributed toward repairs. Lü Yan leaped down the steps and grabbed him by the collar. “Where is the timber you repaired it with? On the roof of your own house?”

Suo Gong shouted for him to let go and seized the account book. He did not declare Feng guilty of embezzlement on the spot. First he sent the field assessors to examine the rice paddies and wheat fields, and had the runners measure the water held upstream. The young wheat in the east ditch was already scorched dry; another half day would likely cost the downstream farmers an entire harvest. The upstream rice could hold out another night. Suo Gong ordered the east ditch opened for two hours, the flow diverted to the southern ditch that evening, and the upstream supply replenished after midnight. Lü Yan protested. The magistrate told him to accompany the assessors and see the shoots for himself.
“I’ve fought in wars,” Lü Yan said.
“I know.”
“My family was awarded its fields for military service.”
“I know.”
“Then why give the former Yan people water first?”
“When you see their shoots dying sooner than yours, you will know.”

Lü Yan watched the magistrate for a moment, then at last ordered the lock removed from the winch. Water rushed beneath the sluice. Farmers on both banks of the east ditch ran beside it, fearful that some board upstream might be lowered again. Suo Gong left runners to guard the sluice and sent Feng to the county jail. Still the villagers were uneasy: upstream families left men to watch the hours, downstream families posted guards at the southern mouth, and Liang Wuzhi even ate his supper on the stone steps.

That night the magistrate gathered the disputing parties at the ward headman’s house to discuss rebuilding the sluice. The county storehouse would furnish the timber, while labor days would be assessed according to the actual acreage of irrigated fields. The water-turn register would be copied three times: one posted beside the sluice, one held at the county office, and one kept at the village school. Three canal stewards would be chosen, one each from upstream, the middle reaches and downstream. No gate could be unlocked on a county clerk’s private paper alone.
“What if the three men collude?” Lü Yan asked.
“Then bring a complaint to the county.”
“What if the county takes bribes too?”
“There are censors in Ye.”
“And if the censors take bribes?”
“Then send your petition to Chang’an.” Suo Gong rubbed his brow wearily. “If what you want is one man who can never be corrupt, you won’t find him in my county.”
Tuoba Lin tapped the table. “If we need three men, why not choose one from each people? One from Yan, one from Guanzhong and one from the Qiang, each holding a token.”
Liang Wuzhi raised his head. “If a Qiang lives upstream, which side am I to speak for when we divide the water?”
“Your own people, of course.”
“But my fields are downstream.”

The room went quiet. Someone fed the fire by the stove; its light fell across Liang Wuzhi’s crippled leg. Slowly he said, “The canal water changes every year, but the houses remain. So do you and I. If I care only for the Qiang when we repair the canal, who will open the southern gate for my grandson after I am gone?”

His words were plain, but hard to refute. The argument dragged on until the third watch before the villagers reluctantly agreed to rotate water according to drought and acreage. Military merit would bring no extra hours, nor would long residence under Yan. The damaged old sluice was to be replaced within seven days.
When A-Luo returned home, Lady Zhao still had a lamp burning. She brought her son porridge, saw the marks on his face and asked first, “Who hit you this time?”
“I struck first.”
“So studying hasn’t cured your temper.”

A-Luo asked why the clan had once refused to acknowledge him, and why boys at school still mocked him over it. Lady Zhao did not answer at once. She reached out and brushed the hair at his temple. “While your father lived, everyone said you were one of the Helai family. Now he is gone, they are all busy deciding which half of you does not belong. Why should you help them decide?”
A-Luo stared into his bowl for a long while without speaking.
“Do you want to go back and fight that Fu boy again?” she asked.
“No more fighting.”
“That’s progress.”
“I have to copy the section on assault tomorrow. My hand hurts.”
Mother and son laughed together until the porridge had gone cold.

Near the end of the fourth watch, a gong sounded at the sluice. First came the dull crack of splitting wood. Then the winch spun wildly, its iron chain lashing against the stone wall in showers of sparks. The rotten gate boards burst under the full weight of the stored water. The east ditch could not contain it; the flood leaped the bank and surged toward the village school and the low mud houses. A guard at the sluice took a blow to the shoulder from the chain and stumbled out, shouting until his voice tore.
“The canal has burst!”

Lü Yan arrived in nothing but his undershirt. Seeing the elm crossbeam had torn free of the sluice slot, he immediately ordered his own cattle shed dismantled. Tuoba Lin ran up, glanced at it and cursed that its timbers were too short. He ordered his kin to pull down the frame of their family’s grain barn instead. Together the men hauled a long beam to the water’s edge, sinking into soft mud with every step. Liang Wuzhi dragged several coils of rope out of his house, wound the ends around a locust tree and told the strongest swimmers to tie the ropes around their waists before entering the ditch.

Suo Gong arrived in the night. Disregarding old rules about the county granary, he ordered the clerks to empty relief-grain sacks and fill them with earth to block the breach in the east ditch. The granary keeper followed with his ledger, demanding to know who would answer for the lost sacks. Suo Gong snatched one from him. “Put it against the county. Put it under my name. Tomorrow I’ll explain it to Ye myself.”

Standing on higher ground, A-Luo shouted “Left!” in Xianbei, then called in Chinese for the southern spillway to be opened. In his urgency he tangled the two languages until no one could understand him. Liang Wuzhi shouted angrily, “Just say three words: 'Open the south gate!'”

A-Luo changed to the shortest commands he could manage, and more than a hundred people began digging southward. Yet the roar of the flood was not subdued by human shouting. The first line of straw sacks washed away as soon as it entered the water; the second tilted sideways. A Guanzhong soldier was swept off his feet. Tuoba Lin lunged to grab him and was dragged in as well. The rope snapped taut. Only when Liang Wuzhi and a dozen others hauled with all their strength were both men pulled ashore. The rescued soldier coughed up muddy water, recognized Tuoba Lin and cursed weakly, “Why did it have to be you, you Yan barbarian?”
Tuoba Lin laughed through his coughing. “Shouldn’t have saved you, then.”

Before noon they finally forced the beam across the sluice slot, and earth-filled sacks diverted the water into the southern branch. Three low houses in Xinmin Ward lost their mud walls; half the school floor was waterlogged, and more than a dozen people were injured. Fortunately no one died. Lü Yan stood barefoot in the mud, his soles cut by splintered wood, and Tuoba Lin tossed him a roll of dry cloth. Liang Wuzhi leaned against a tree, his chest still heaving. The insults they had once traded suddenly seemed less important after someone had held fast to a rope for them in the flood.

They had barely recovered their breath when a field assessor examining the breach picked up a damaged wooden wedge. Fresh marks from a narrow axe scored its surface. Confusion broke out anew. Had former Yan people secretly opened the water? Had Guanzhong men deliberately smashed the canal? Some even stared at Liang Wuzhi’s lame leg and declared the Qiang must have broken the sluice in protest against the water schedule.

Liang Wuzhi dragged himself upright against the tree, his hands shaking with fury. “Yesterday, if I hadn’t pulled that rope, some of you would be at the bottom of the ditch. If you insist on searching Qiang homes today, start with mine.”

Suo Gong ordered the broken wood sealed as evidence, and forbade anyone to lay hands on another. At dusk, a farmer named Guo Sheng came to the county office of his own accord carrying a narrow axe. He lived at the very end of the eastern ditch; twelve mu of his wheat had gone without water for three days. His wife had died of illness the previous year, leaving two children in his care. Officer Feng had previously let water through only for those who could pay his private grain levy. Guo could not pay. Even when he heard the night before that the new rules would rotate the water, he did not believe it would ever reach his household.
“I only meant to open a crack,” he said. “Let a little through, then close it again before dawn. How was I to know all the wood inside was rotten?”

Kneeling in the hall, he held an axe that matched the wedge found by the assessor. When Lü Yan heard, he rushed in so angry that he meant to beat the man where he knelt. Suo Gong barred his way. “He damaged a public sluice and endangered others. That must be tried. If you beat him to death, I shall have to try you too.”

The inquiry also settled Feng’s accounts. For years he had collected grain and money privately, falsified inspections and sold the timber allocated by the court for sluice repairs to estates. Then he frightened each side with tales of “Yan households making trouble,” “Guanzhong veterans taking too much water,” or “incomplete Qiang registrations,” forcing all of them to pay. The county recovered the illicit proceeds under law and ordered compensation for the losses; the penal judgment would be submitted separately for review by the commandery. Guo Sheng, who had illegally damaged a public sluice and endangered his neighbors, was sentenced to work on canal repairs to make restitution; the medical expenses of injured households were to be apportioned under law. His two young children’s claim to their fields was not erased because their father had committed a crime.

The judgments were posted beside the north canal. Downstream people said Guo had only been trying to save his wheat, and five years of canal labor was too harsh. Upstream people said he had nearly drowned others, and five years was too lenient. Feng protested his innocence while sending petitions to his former patron, but no one wished to account for the beams he had sold. Helping the county copy the testimony, A-Luo found that one labor entry on the sluice repairs had been misdated by three days. When he brought it back for correction, an old clerk rebuked him for needless fuss. A-Luo answered that if they left it wrong, someone next year would say the laborers had never come at all. The clerk stared at him for a long time, then took up his brush and recopied the page.

Seven days later work began on the new sluice. Hearing that iron fittings were needed, the merchant caravan from Guzang returned and unloaded its wares. Merchant Kang laughingly asked when the magistrate would pay the balance. Suo Gong carefully secured the inspection voucher and told him that, if payment was delayed, he could take it to the commandery to demand settlement. Kang did not quite believe him, but left the iron hoops anyway. “Better than having no one to claim a debt from.”

The three canal stewards were appointed: Lü Yan upstream, Liang Wuzhi in the middle, and Tuoba Lin downstream. Each had a wooden token; the lock could be opened only when the tokens were brought together. On the first water turn Lü Yan arrived half a day late, saying a cow was ill, and Liang Wuzhi docked his wages according to the register. Lü Yan cursed a little but still put his seal to the entry. On the second turn Tuoba Lin tried to secure an extra half-hour for the eastern ditch. Lü Yan refused, following the drought assessment made by the field officials, and Tuoba was so angry that he refused to drink with him for two days. The new sluice held firm. Human partiality had not been dismantled along with the rotten timbers.

When classes resumed at the commandery school, A-Luo made three copies of the new water-turn register. One was posted at the sluice, one kept at the county office, and the third hung in the classroom. The swelling on Fu Sheng’s nose had gone down. Seeing A-Luo enter with bamboo slips, he said first, “You people even need three copies of a list to let water flow?”
“Don’t people fight over water where you come from?”
“They do.”
“How often do you fight?”

Fu Sheng considered it, then laughed and helped him fix the wooden hook to the wall. From his seat at the front, Instructor Pei saw the two boys carrying a bookshelf shoulder to shoulder. He neither praised them nor revived their quarrel, but told them to mend the paper over the windows so the next rain would not wet the books again.

That evening Lady Zhao accompanied a young woman to the school to borrow a clerk’s desk. The woman carried a baby barely a month old. The child’s father had died young. The father’s clan wanted the baby to bear its surname, the mother’s family wanted its own, and the Xianbei grandmother insisted on an old name. The young woman was anxious: next month the county would distribute grain for planting to widowed households, and without a household page the baby would not count as another mouth.
A-Luo spread clean paper before them. The county clerk lifted his brush. “What is the child’s name?”
“Lu An,” the mother said.
“A-Liujuan,” said the grandmother.

They had spoken almost at once. They argued until the startled baby began crying. The old woman rocked and soothed the child without yielding. A-Luo looked at the tiny red face and remembered standing with his mother in a hall in Chang’an seven years before, when a clan elder had held the saber once worn by his father. Everyone had fought over those eighty mu of land; no one had been willing to say first that the child had a right to farm them.

He told the clerk, “Write down both names. Use the name reported by the mother as the primary entry for now, and record the old name as an alias. If they wish to change it later, let them follow the Household Statutes.”
The grandmother would have argued on, but the young mother had tears in her eyes. “Just write it down. The planting grain matters more.”

The clerk entered the date of birth, the relatives and the property awaiting verification. The principal register still gave the family’s state as Qin; the old people’s place of origin was recorded on a supplementary page. A-Luo supported the baby while the woman collected her papers. A little hand emerged from the swaddling and grasped his forefinger, astonishingly warm. He felt suddenly like laughing, though his eyes stung.

When the ink dried, the woman folded the household page and tucked it into the inner folds of the baby’s swaddling. The grandmother asked, “If the court changes one day, will they still recognize that piece of paper?”

A-Luo met her eyes. He did not offer the promise that no one could make. “Then take this paper and ask the new officials. The county has a duplicate register, and so does the commandery. That’s better than having no proof at all.”
The grandmother tucked the swaddling close and nodded to him.

Outside, it was time to change the water at the north canal. Lü Yan, Tuoba Lin and Liang Wuzhi stood beside the sluice. The three wooden tokens were fitted one by one into the lock, the winch turned, and clear water flowed slowly toward the southern ditch. An old Di blade still hung beneath Lü Yan’s eaves; in a chest of Tuoba Lin’s lay coins minted under Yan; on memorial days Liang Wuzhi still poured wine westward for his dead. The children knew nothing of the weight of those old things. They were racing after a white goose, which ran into Lü Yan’s onion patch and trampled several rows of tender shoots, bringing the old man out to wave his stick and curse halfway down the lane.

After seeing the women off, A-Luo stood at the school door. The rush of the north canal mingled with children’s laughter, and caravan bells sounded faintly from the main road. He went back inside, placed the newly completed household entry in its wooden compartment, and wrote the date on which it should next be checked. His brushwork was still uncertain. One downward stroke had run too long, so he dipped his brush again and made it clear.

Far away someone called “Helai A-Luo,” and another child shouted “Brother A-Luo!” He answered and rose to see whether enough water had reached the ditch by his mother’s house. The bamboo slips laid out to dry that afternoon had yet to be gathered in. Beneath the eaves was the scent of ink, and the light slowly faded. Cooking smoke rose over Xinmin Ward. Every household had come from somewhere different; tonight all of them would heat water and cook their evening meal on this same ground.

Lady Zhao was sorting beans by the doorway when she saw her son. Her first question was whether he had eaten his midday meal. A-Luo spread out a thin sheet issued by the commandery school. His name was written there, with the statutes and arithmetic he was studying. Lady Zhao could read few characters, but she traced both official marks with her finger. She remembered holding him in her arms in that hall years ago. Everyone had argued over the eighty mu, yet no one had been willing to speak the child’s name first.

“Are the fields still ours?” she asked. A-Luo answered yes, rolled up the paper and went to clear the silt from the narrow ditch at the corner of the yard. At nightfall she left his supper beside the stove. When he returned from reading, it was still warm.
